summary.en: A deep artist roster makes Motown Hitsville U.S.A. in substance as well as in name.
summary.zh: 实力雄厚的艺人阵容，令Motown成为名副其实的“美国热单镇”。

body.zh:
实力雄厚的艺人阵容，令Motown成为名副其实的“美国热单镇”。

现在来讲讲Motown旗下的艺人。我们将关注其巅峰岁月，即64年到66年之间；与此同期，在1965年的夏天，The Beatles首次大获成功，美国歌手开始予以回应。
回忆上一章我们谈到的东西，有民谣摇滚、《Mr. Tambourine Man》和Dylan等等；以及早期Motown取得成功，其首批艺人纷纷登上榜单。除了此前已提到的人物，还有唱《Please Mr. Postman》的The Marvelette、The Contours和Smokey Robinson and the Miracles等。Smokey Robinson不只是Motown的歌手或制作人，其自己也是一位艺人。他的组合有首歌成为了1960年R&B榜单的冠军和流行榜单的亚军，歌名叫《Shop Around》。最初他们录完这首歌之后，Berry Gordy把录音带回了家； 我不知道他当时拿的是盘式磁带，还是醋酸纤维唱片——后者是一种临时的小型唱片，你可以在上面刻录声音、放到唱片机上播放，但它在播放十几遍后就会损坏。不过它确实是临时检验录音成果的好办法。总之，Berry Gordy当晚在家里听了录音，而他认定这个录音的节奏弄错了。于是他召集了The Miracles的所有人：“我们得重录。” 大家问： “明天吗？” 他说：“不，现在！” 就这样，他把大家都赶出了被窝。他们到达录音室时已经是半夜了。由于找不到原来的录音室钢琴手，所以后来唱片里的钢琴部分其实是Berry Gordy亲自弹的。他们调整了节奏，而新的录音就是后来成为了热门单曲的版本。想想看，Berry Gordy就是如此专注于这项事业；要是决定了发行某张唱片，他就会不惜在最后时刻把大家喊来、将录音完全重做一遍，只因自己不确定原来的节奏是否正确。这就是Berry Gordy Jr.在早年对于Motown的全心投入。说到Smokey Robinson and the Miracles，其另一支早年热门歌曲是1962年的《You've Really Got a Hold On Me》。这首歌在R&B榜单排名第1位，在流行榜单排名第8位。The Beatles也翻唱过这首歌曲。在他们的头几张专辑里，不少翻唱内容都源自Motown的唱片。Motown的另一个早期明星，是1962年的Mary Wells。她有首相当热门的歌曲叫《The One Who Really Loves You》。而她最为人熟知的作品，我想是1964年的《My Guy》，这首歌拿到了流行榜单的冠军。
至于其他的艺人，我想先从Holland-Dozier-Holland负责制作的那些谈起。Holland-Dozier-Holland（HDH），这个专事歌曲创作、制作的小组，是60年代中期最成功的流行乐创作、制作团队之一。他们能和Bob Dylan、The Byrds、The Beatles、The Rolling Stones等人物并论，其都在60年代中期，也即65、66年左右，取得了巨大的成功。下面就是一些和Holland-Dozier-Holland合作过的艺人。The Supremes，如果非要选一个组合来代表60年代中期的Motown，那只能是她们了。有些人声称，The Beatles来到美国就把女子组合的音乐赶下了榜单，其实这不完全正确。The Beatles在1964年首获成功之后，不仅Phil Spector手下的女子组合推出过热门歌曲，大受欢迎的The Supremes也是纯粹的女子组合。她们自1964年起开始取得巨大成功，并将势头一直延续到60年代末期。虽然并不属于那批来自纽约录音室的女子组合，但来自底特律的她们同样做得很好。所以论及The Beatles的介入与英伦入侵，虽然那确实是重要的转折点，但也要知道它并未改变一切。总之，The Supremes非常重要。我们熟知的组合阵容是Diana Ross、Mary Wilson和Florence Ballard。该组合最早叫做The Primetets，因为那时The Temptations还叫做The Primes，或者说那时有个最终会改名为The Temptations的组合叫做The Primes。可以说The Supremes是与The Temptations相对应的女子组合。她们整天在录音室附近打转，希望能出一张唱片。而Berry Gordy Jr.曾明确告诉她们，回家去把高中读完，然后我们再来考虑唱片的事。她们确实出过几张反响平平的唱片，那时在Motown这边，她们被称为“不走红至上组合”（the no hit Supremes）。到了某个时刻，Berry Gordy决定让Diana Ross担任主唱。从技术层面讲，她的声音并不是组合里最强有力的；但Berry Gordy从她的声音中发现了某种潜质和能量。我认为，他指的是歌声里的性感气息和传情达意的能力。他发现了这一点，并决定让Diana Ross做所有歌曲的主唱。然后，他让她们试着和Holland-Dozier-Holland合作；到了第三回合作，The Supremes就在1964年夏天凭借《Where Did Our Love Go》拿下了榜单冠军。它登上冠军位置的时间，正值The Beatles发行《A Hard Day's Night》，也即所有人都深陷披头士狂热(Beatlemania)的时候。所以说，The Beatles和The Supremes简直是针锋相对、并驾齐驱。就像The Beatles和The Rolling Stones一样，The Supremes也取得过榜单五连冠，包括1964年的《Baby Love》、《Come See About Me》，以及1965年的《Stop! In the Name of Love》和《Back in My Arms Again》。她们的巨大成功一直延续到60年代末期。当然，在70年代Motown搬到洛杉矶、更多地涉足电影行业之后，Diana Ross又收获了一段成功的个人音乐事业。
当年另一个和Holland-Dozier-Holland合作的组合叫做Four Tops。与HDH合作的女子组合有The Supremes，而男子组合方面，如果你要找一个对应者，那就是Four Tops了。Four Tops成立于1954年，曾和芝加哥的Chess唱片签约；到1964年，他们转来Motown，以Levi Stubbs为主唱。在HDH的编排下，他们的歌曲里常常包含有趣的管弦乐片段；和The Supremes、The Temptations、Martha and The Vandellas等组合相比，Four Tops的唱片里有着更多的管弦乐。如果你在寻找Four Tops的代表作，下面这些歌曲就不容错过了：在1964年排名第11的《Baby I Need Your Loving》；我的私人最爱之一《I Can't Help Myself》——它又称《Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch》，在1965年的流行榜单和R&B榜单都拿下了第一；《Standing in the Shadows of Love》，在1966年，同样登上了两个榜单的首位。那么，这些就是60年代中期 HDH和Four Tops合力推出的好歌。
HDH也和Martha and the Vandellas合作。该组合的主唱Martha Reeves最初是一名职业歌手，后来这个身份也一直伴随着她，但她入职Motown时的身份并非歌手，而是秘书。所以当时Martha Reeves一方面负责商务上的打字、接电话，另一方面又在争取与Motown签订唱片合同，毕竟她晚上还会到俱乐部驻唱。终于她得到了一个唱和声的机会，是1962年Marvin Gaye《Stubborn Kind of Fellow》的和声。不论如何，她的组合Martha and the Vandellas 有过一首热门歌曲《Heat Wave》，其同样由HDH制作出品，在1963年登上了流行榜单的第4位和R&B榜单的第1位。然后，在The Beatles踏入这个国家之前，“Mickey” Stevenson接手了这个组合，并为其创作了歌曲《Dancing in the Street》；说来讽刺，它是Martha and the Vandellas最有名的作品，在1964年却只拿到榜单第二名。然后HDH再次接手该组合，两者合作推出了1965年的《Nowhere to Run》 和1967年的《Jimmy Mack》等热门单曲。
其他艺人则与多个制作人有过合作。实际上，Berry Gordy Jr.的做法就是让艺人和制作人配对，等到双方已经无法合作推出热单，他会找来另一个制作人或歌曲作者，看看新的人员能不能给艺人带来好运。The Temptations可能是最出名的例子之一。刚才讲The Supremes时曾提到，他们最初的名字是The Primes。事实上，它是由两个团体合并而来的：The Primes和 The Distance，共同组成了The Temptations。他们因其舞蹈编排而出名，组内五个男孩都能跳出精彩的舞步；但这也让他们和Charlie Atkins产生了摩擦，后者认为自己有权安排Motown所有艺人的编舞，而The Temptations更希望坚持自己原有的风格。这其中就存在一些摩擦，双方在舞步设计上互不谦让。相比其他组合，The Temptations的舞步更为健美，也更为张扬。他们正因此而出名。谈及The Temptations的舞步，应该将其和James Brown联系起来——之后我们会谈到James Brown——James Brown的舞步和The Temptations有相似之处，而到了70、80年代，他最终也成为了The Jackson 5和Michael Jackson的模仿对象。所以，正因为The Temptations既有好歌、也有好的表演和舞蹈，他们才能成为一个极具影响力的组合。起初，大概在60年代中段这个黄金时期，David Ruffin和Eddie Kendricks 担任该组合的主唱，后者的高音假声尤为突出。我在上一章讲过东西两岸的高音歌手代表，西岸是The Beach Boys的Brian Wilson，东岸是The Four Seasons的Frankie Valli；而Motown则有Eddie Kendricks，他可以说是该领域内的第三号人物。由Smokey Robinson写作、制作，在1964年排名第11位的《The Way You Do the Things You Do》，尤其能够表明上述事实。Smokey继续与The Temptations合作推出热门单曲，包括在1965年同时夺得流行榜单和R&B榜单的冠军的《My Girl》。此后他有些走了下坡路，于是Berry Gordy Jr.将The Temptations交给了Norman Whitfield。60年代末到70年代，该组合都在Whitfield的带领下前进。《Ain't Too Proud to Beg》在1966年登上了R&B榜单的首位和流行榜单的第13位。同年《I Know I'm Losing You》在R&B榜单上排名第1位，在流行榜单上排名第8位。所以The Temptations是60年代中期Motown成功艺人里的又一个好例子。
Marvin Gaye是另一位曾与多个Motown制作人合作的杰出歌手。他们合作推出了不少热门单曲，比如“Mickey” Stevenson在1963年制作的《Pride and Joy》；1965年的《How Sweet to Be Loved By You》由HDH为他制作；同年的另一首歌曲《Ain't That Peculiar》则来自Smokey Robinson。之后讲到70年代黑人流行乐的时候，我们会谈到更多关于Marvin Gaye的事情，因为他的专辑《What's Going On》不仅是黑人流行乐史上的重要作品，也是Motown推出的第一张概念专辑。届时我们还会讲到Stevie Wonder，以及其他自主参与唱片制作的歌手。这对于此时的Motown来说还是很少见的，正常来讲制作人、艺人和录音室乐队 都有各自的分工，彼此互不干涉。
最后就来简要地谈谈Stevie Wonder。他在Motown以童星身份出道，负责唱歌和吹口琴。最初人们并未将其视为歌曲作者或制作人，这对我们来说确实有点奇怪，因为如今大家都认为他是全能的音乐才子。但当时他就是一个艺人，无非唱唱歌、吹吹口琴。他的第一首热门歌曲，《Fingertips, Pt. 2》，在1963年同时占据了流行榜单和R&B榜单的首位。其实这首歌是无意中录下来的。换言之，它是一次现场表演的录音；由于反响很好，最终才得以作为唱片出版。事实上，这次录音非常随意，贝斯手一度离开了舞台，为配合下一个登台艺人做准备。我想这个艺人大概是Mary Wells之类的，因为Motown的组合都会在同一个节目上登台表演。你可以在录音里听到贝斯手跑回舞台、拿起他的贝斯，然后询问：“弹哪个调？” 这样他就能快速加入到歌曲中来。无论如何，它是Stevie Wonder的大热歌曲，饱含Stevie Wonder的热情和能量。他借此在电视广播上首获成功。Berry Gordy Jr.也在歌曲制作人之列，但正如我所说，这首歌曲从未经过棚内录制。1966年，“Mickey” Stevenson制作了《Uptight (Everything is Alright) 》，其是Stevie Wonder的另一首热门，占据了R&B榜单以及流行榜单的首位。我曾说过，Stevie Wonder和Marvin Gaye 是我们将在本课程的第二部分予以详谈的人物。对于1970年代的黑人流行乐，他们是极其重要的人物，其影响比之在60年代更要突出。
我们对Motown的讨论大致如上。下一节，我们将转向孟菲斯，去看看比肩Motown的南方灵魂乐中心，也即Stax——或者采用他们自己的说法，称之为美国灵魂乐镇（Soulsville, USA）。
body.en:
A deep artist roster makes Motown Hitsville U.S.A. in substance as well as in name.

Now Motown’s artists. We focus on the peak years, 1964–66—alongside summer 1965, when the Beatles first triumph and American artists begin to answer.
Recall the last chapter: folk rock, “Mr. Tambourine Man,” Dylan, and so on; plus early Motown success as first artists hit the charts. Beyond those already named: the Marvelettes with “Please Mr. Postman,” the Contours, Smokey Robinson and the Miracles. Smokey is not only Motown singer or producer—he is an artist in his own right. His group has a 1960 No. 1 R&B / No. 2 pop hit, “Shop Around.” After they first cut it, Berry Gordy takes the recording home—whether reel tape or an acetate (a temporary small disc you can cut and play until it wears out after a dozen plays; still a good way to check a take). That night he decides the groove is wrong. He calls every Miracle: we have to recut. Tomorrow? No—now. He hauls them out of bed. They reach the studio around midnight. The original studio pianist cannot be found, so the piano on the hit is Gordy himself. They fix the tempo; the new take becomes the smash. That is how focused Gordy is early on: if he decides a record goes out, he will call everyone at the last minute and remake the whole thing because he is unsure about the groove. Another early Miracles hit is 1962’s “You’ve Really Got a Hold on Me”—No. 1 R&B, No. 8 pop. The Beatles cover it too; several early Beatles album covers come from Motown. Another early Motown star is Mary Wells in 1962—“The One Who Really Loves You” is a big hit; her best-known may be 1964’s “My Guy,” a pop No. 1.
Other artists: start with those Holland–Dozier–Holland produce. HDH is one of the mid-1960s’ most successful writer–producer teams—worth naming alongside Dylan, the Byrds, Beatles, Stones, all huge around 1965–66. Artists who work with them: the Supremes. If you must pick one act for mid-1960s Motown, it is them. Some claim the Beatles’ arrival knocks girl-group music off the charts; that is not fully true. After the Beatles’ 1964 breakthrough, Phil Spector’s girl groups still score hits, and the hugely popular Supremes are a pure girl group. Success from 1964 runs into the late 1960s. Not New York studio girl groups, but Detroit—and they do well. The Beatles and the Invasion are a major turn, but they do not change everything. The Supremes matter. The familiar lineup is Diana Ross, Mary Wilson, Florence Ballard. Early on they are the Primettes, because the Temptations are still the Primes—or a group that will become the Temptations is called the Primes. The Supremes are the female counterpart. They hang around the studio hoping for a record. Gordy tells them plainly: finish high school, then we talk records. They cut a few flat records; Motown calls them “the no-hit Supremes.” At some point Gordy makes Diana Ross lead. Technically her voice is not the strongest in the group; he hears potential and energy—sexual charge and the ability to communicate feeling. He puts her on every lead, pairs them with HDH; by the third try, summer 1964’s “Where Did Our Love Go” is a No. 1—same stretch as the Beatles’ A Hard Day’s Night and Beatlemania. Beatles and Supremes go head to head. Like Beatles and Stones, the Supremes take five straight No. 1s, including 1964’s “Baby Love,” “Come See About Me,” and 1965’s “Stop! In the Name of Love” and “Back in My Arms Again.” The run lasts into the late 1960s. In the 1970s, after Motown moves to L.A. and into film, Diana Ross also builds a solo career.
Another HDH act: the Four Tops. HDH’s girl group is the Supremes; the male counterpart is the Four Tops. Formed 1954, once on Chess in Chicago; 1964 they come to Motown with Levi Stubbs on lead. Under HDH their records often carry interesting orchestral touches—more orchestra than Supremes, Temptations, Martha and the Vandellas. Key tracks: 1964’s “Baby I Need Your Loving” (No. 11); a personal favorite, “I Can’t Help Myself” (“Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch”), No. 1 pop and R&B in 1965; “Standing in the Shadows of Love,” No. 1 on both charts in 1966. Mid-1960s HDH–Four Tops material.
HDH also work Martha and the Vandellas. Lead Martha Reeves starts as a professional singer and keeps that identity, but she joins Motown as a secretary—typing, phones—while chasing a recording deal and singing clubs at night. She gets a background shot on Marvin Gaye’s 1962 “Stubborn Kind of Fellow.” The group’s hit “Heat Wave,” also HDH, is No. 4 pop / No. 1 R&B in 1963. Before the Beatles enter the country, “Mickey” Stevenson takes the group and writes “Dancing in the Street”—ironically their best-known song, only No. 2 in 1964. HDH return for 1965’s “Nowhere to Run” and 1967’s “Jimmy Mack,” among other hits.
Other artists work with multiple producers. Gordy’s method is to pair artist and producer until the hits stop, then try another writer or producer for luck. The Temptations are a famous case. As noted with the Supremes, they begin as the Primes—actually a merger of the Primes and the Distants. They are famous for choreography; all five dance brilliantly—which creates friction with Cholly Atkins, who thinks he owns Motown choreography while the Temptations want their own style. Their moves are more athletic and flashy than other Motown acts—that is their reputation. Link their dancing to James Brown—we will cover him—similar mobility; by the 1970s–80s he also becomes a model for the Jackson 5 and Michael Jackson. Strong songs plus strong show and dance make them influential. In the mid-1960s golden stretch David Ruffin and Eddie Kendricks share leads; Kendricks’s high falsetto stands out. Last chapter’s high-voice markers: west-coast Brian Wilson, east-coast Frankie Valli; Motown has Kendricks as a third. Smokey’s 1964 “The Way You Do the Things You Do” (No. 11) shows it. Smokey keeps scoring with them, including 1965’s “My Girl,” No. 1 pop and R&B. Then he slips; Gordy hands the Temptations to Norman Whitfield. Late 1960s into the 1970s they move under Whitfield. “Ain’t Too Proud to Beg” is No. 1 R&B / No. 13 pop in 1966; same year “I Know I’m Losing You” is No. 1 R&B / No. 8 pop. Another mid-1960s Motown success story.
Marvin Gaye works with several Motown producers and scores hits: Mickey Stevenson’s 1963 “Pride and Joy”; HDH’s 1965 “How Sweet It Is to Be Loved by You”; Smokey’s 1965 “Ain’t That Peculiar.” In Part Two on 1970s Black pop we will say more—What’s Going On is a landmark and Motown’s first concept album. We will also cover Stevie Wonder and other artists who take part in production. That is still rare at Motown then; normally producer, artist, and studio band keep separate lanes.
Finally a brief word on Stevie Wonder. He arrives as a child star—singing and harmonica. At first no one sees him as writer or producer—odd to us now, when he is the all-around genius—but then he is simply an artist who sings and plays harp. First hit: “Fingertips, Pt. 2,” No. 1 pop and R&B in 1963. It is recorded almost by accident—a live take that works so well it becomes a release. Very casual: the bassist leaves the stage to prep for the next Motown act (Mary Wells, perhaps—Motown packages share bills). You hear him run back, grab the bass, ask “What key?” and jump in. Anyway it is a Stevie smash, full of energy, and his first TV/radio breakthrough. Gordy is among the credited producers, but as I said it is never a studio cut. In 1966 Mickey Stevenson produces “Uptight (Everything’s Alright),” another hit, No. 1 R&B and pop. I have said Stevie Wonder and Marvin Gaye belong mainly to Part Two. For 1970s Black pop they matter even more than in the 1960s.
That is roughly our Motown discussion. Next we turn to Memphis—the southern-soul center rivaling Motown: Stax, or in their own words, Soulsville, U.S.A.
